title: A Startup Wants to Fight AI Bioweapons With AI
gist: Radical Numerics, a 2025 San Francisco startup from the Stanford team behind the Evo DNA models, launched Omnii Defense, an offline edge AI model that scores genome sequences for natural or AI-engineered threat risk, pitching an AI-vs-AI biodefense arms race akin to cybersecurity. The tool is limited to vetted testers under evaluation by national labs and agencies, while outside experts caution detection is not proof of real threat, and the company faces a governance blemish after adviser George Church resigned over a partner-disclosure omission.

insights.claim: Radical Numerics announced Omnii Defense, an offline-capable edge AI model that flags natural and AI-engineered pathogens using a laptop and a portable USB gene sequencer, aimed at researchers and public health officials in the field.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Positions a young AI-bio startup in the government/public-health biosecurity procurement market; watch for agency contracts.

insights.claim: Omnii Defense outputs a single 0-to-1 'threat score' per genome sequence, combining the likelihood a sequence is unnatural with functional predictions, plus pathogenicity, AI-generation and taxonomy estimates.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A single risk score is a product format that maps onto screening/compliance workflows, a potential recurring-revenue use case.
insights.locator: Omnii Defense, the company's latest tool

insights.claim: Access to Omnii Defense is limited to vetted external testers, and Radical Numerics says national laboratories, government agencies and independent evaluators are assessing the model's performance.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Product is pre-commercial; government validation results are the key catalyst before any revenue or contracts.
insights.locator: Access to Omnii Defense is currently limited

insights.claim: Radical Numerics CEO Eric Nguyen frames biodefense as heading into an AI-driven arms race similar to cybersecurity, where attackers and defenders both use AI to gain an edge, and argues biosecurity defense has lagged far behind.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: If the cybersecurity analogy holds, AI biosecurity could become a defense-spending category with vendor demand driven by frontier-AI risk.
insights.quote: We felt that the biosecurity space was far behind on the defense side,

insights.claim: Frontier AI labs have themselves warned their models could help develop bioweapons, which creates the demand narrative for AI-based biodefense tools even though many scientists consider AI-made bioweapons a low-likelihood threat.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Market demand rests partly on a contested threat model; policy sentiment toward AI risk will drive budgets more than realized incidents.

insights.claim: Broad Institute's Bronwyn MacInnis endorses using AI to stay ahead of malicious actors but cautions that detecting a signal is far from determining whether a pathogen has real consequence or was engineered, limiting how far detection tools can be relied on.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Expect buyers to demand evidence of real-world actionability; detection alone may not justify large procurement.

insights.claim: Existing federally funded biodefense tools such as Felix (Finding Engineering-Linked Indicators) match sequences against libraries of known organisms, whereas Radical Numerics pitches Omnii as predictive rather than lookup-based, which it argues catches threats that cataloged matching misses.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Predictive AI models could displace or supplement legacy government-funded screening tools; incumbency of federal programs is a sales hurdle.

insights.claim: In a company-run held-out test, Omnii still flagged 33% of sequences of a withheld outbreak virus as pathogenic with the species removed from training and 22% with the whole genus removed, while non-AI tools gave essentially no risk signal, per head of biodefense Christine Parthemore.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Self-reported benchmark that is a marketing proof point; independent evaluation by labs/agencies is needed to confirm.

insights.claim: Radical Numerics' head of biodefense Christine Parthemore calls Omnii a 'step change' for biodefense.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Company messaging targets a category-defining position; the claim is vendor-sourced.
insights.locator: Christine Parthemore, Radical Numerics' head of biodefense

insights.claim: Radical Numerics is a San Francisco-based startup founded in 2025 by Stanford researchers behind the open-source Evo and Evo-2 DNA foundation models, giving it credibility from a known open-source model lineage.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Founding team pedigree in open-source bio foundation models is the startup's main asset; no funding figures were disclosed in the article.

insights.claim: Radical Numerics' broader Omnii genome language model, which spans multiple biological data types beyond DNA, was used in October in a therapeutic project for a patient treated under special FDA permission, extending the company beyond biodefense into therapeutics.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: Dual market exposure (therapeutics plus biodefense) broadens the platform story for investors.
insights.locator: The San Francisco–based company recently made waves

insights.claim: Harvard geneticist George Church resigned as an adviser to Radical Numerics after the company failed to disclose AI biotech startup Tabula Bioscience's involvement in its October therapeutic announcement; Church advised both firms.
insights.speaker: Emily Mullin
insights.so_what: A disclosure-related advisor departure is a governance/reputational flag for diligence on the startup.
insights.locator: Another AI biotech startup, Tabula Bioscience
